title: Analogies
source: MindSpark Grade 6 Aptitude & Reasoning | Chapter 3: Analogies
learningGoals: Identify the relationship between the first pair in an analogy and apply the same relationship to find the missing word.
Solve number analogies by spotting arithmetic operations or square/cube patterns.
Recognise letter analogies using alphabet position differences.
coreIdeas: Always state the relationship in words before guessing the answer: 'Bird is to Nest as Fish is to __' means 'home of a bird is Nest, so home of a fish is __'.
For number analogies, test: +, -, x, square, cube — whichever keeps the same rule for both pairs.
For letter analogies, convert to positions, find the gap, apply the same gap to the second pair.

workedExamples.solution: Relationship: a Bird lives in a Nest (home). Apply same: a Fish lives in a Pond (or Water/River). Answer: Pond.
workedExamples.concept: Word analogy — object and its home/habitat

workedExamples.solution: 4 squared = 16. Apply same operation: 5 squared = 25. Answer: 25.
A=1, B=2 — forward pair. D=4, C=3 — reversed next two letters. EF forward (5,6) — next two are G=7, H=8 reversed: HG. Answer: HG.
workedExamples.concept: Letter analogy — forward pair followed by reversed next pair

onboarding.coachIntro: Spark explains that analogies are about relationships: if you know how two things connect, you can find what connects two other things the same way.
onboarding.placementRule: Start at Group A. If learner answers Groups A and B instantly, move directly to Group C without the full board demo.

mission.missionPromise: By the end you will see the hidden relationship in any analogy and solve it in under 15 seconds — a superpower for every entrance exam!
mission.successCelebration: Award 'Relationship Spotter' badge after Group D. Final badge is 'Analogy Champion' after Group I.

microLessonPattern: Coach names the relationship type and shows a concrete everyday example.
Coach solves one worked analogy step by step on the board, stating the relationship in plain words first.
Coach reads the practice analogy aloud.
Student attempts before solution is shown.
Instant feedback confirms or repairs with a relationship re-statement.
Review prompt tests one more analogy of the same type.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: 10 to 25 XP per group, increasing from Group A to Group I.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Streak counter visible; one free retry per group.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Word badge at Group B, Number badge at Group D, Letter badge at Group F, Master badge at Group I.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Connection spark animation + XP pulse after each correct answer.

reviewLoop.trigger: Two wrong answers prompt a return to the worked example with a simpler pair.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Offer one everyday analogy (e.g. Pen:Write) before retrying the original.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance after one correct analogy plus successful statement of the relationship.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Any group with an error returns as a warm-up card next session.

uiDirectives.primaryFocus: current analogy card with pair displayed prominently
uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: Both pairs of the analogy and the answer input visible without scrolling.

beats.teacherLine: Hello, future reasoning champion! Today we tackle Analogies — one of the most common question types in every aptitude test, olympiad, and entrance exam. An analogy says: 'these two things have this relationship — now find two other things with the SAME relationship.' Once you learn to spot the 5 key relationship types, every analogy question becomes easy. Let's meet the 5 types: Object-Use, Category, Number, Letter, and Part-Whole!
beats.boardAction: Write 'Analogies — Lesson 3' at the top. List the 5 types with a one-word example each: Object-Use (Pen:Write), Category (Rose:Flower), Number (4:16), Letter (AC:EG), Part-Whole (Page:Book).
beats.checkpointPrompt: Warm-up: Pen : Write :: Brush : ? — what is a Brush used for?
beats.fallbackHint: A Pen is used for Writing. A Brush is used for Painting. That is the Tool-Purpose relationship.

beats.teacherLine: Let me demo a word analogy: Bird : Nest :: Fish : ? Step 1 — I read Pair 1 and state the relationship: 'A Bird lives in a Nest — so the relationship is animal-to-home.' Step 2 — apply to Pair 2: 'A Fish lives in a Pond (or Water).' Answer: Pond. The KEY is always stating the relationship out loud before guessing. That sentence saves you every time!
beats.boardAction: Write 'Bird : Nest :: Fish : ?' Draw a bracket around Bird:Nest, label it 'animal: home'. Draw arrow to Fish:? and write 'same rule: fish:home = ?'. Circle 'Pond'.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Apply the same method: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ? — state the relationship, then give the answer.
beats.expectedStudentResponse: School — a Doctor works in a Hospital, so a Teacher works in a School.
beats.fallbackHint: Ask: where does a Doctor work? Hospital. Apply: where does a Teacher work? School.

svgAnimation.text: Relationship: animal lives in its home

beats.teacherLine: Number analogy demo: 4 : 16 :: 5 : ? I test squaring: 4 squared = 16 — yes! So 5 squared = 25. Done! If squaring did not work, I would test multiply by 4: 4 x 4 = 16 — same answer here, but check pair 2: 5 x 4 = 20. Two possible answers! When that happens, look at the answer choices — only one will be listed. The key skill is testing quickly.
beats.boardAction: Write '4 : 16 :: 5 : ?' Show test table: square (4x4=16, 5x5=25) and multiply by 4 (4x4=16, 5x4=20). Circle 25 as the squaring answer.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Quick test: 9 : 81 :: 11 : ? — test squaring first. What do you get?
beats.fallbackHint: 9 x 9 = 81 — that is squaring. Apply: 11 x 11 = 121.

beats.teacherLine: You have all 5 analogy tools ready. As you work through Groups A to I, use this 3-step method every time: Step 1 — identify the analogy type. Step 2 — state the relationship in a sentence. Step 3 — apply the same relationship to find the answer. Never skip Step 2 — it is your shortcut to accuracy!
beats.boardAction: Display a 3-step method card: (1) Identify type, (2) Say the relationship sentence, (3) Apply to Pair 2. Below list the 5 types as a reference strip.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Before Groups start: which 3-step do you do FIRST — identify type, state relationship, or apply?
beats.fallbackHint: Step 1 is always: identify the analogy type (word, number, letter, part-whole, or tool-purpose).

svgAnimation.text: Step 2: Say the relationship in one sentence
Step 3: Apply the same sentence to Pair 2

sessionFlow.coachHook: Analogies are all about relationships! Bird : Nest — a bird lives in a nest. So Fish : ? — a fish lives in… what? Same relationship, different objects. That's all an analogy is!

boardDemo.title: Object Analogy — Home Relationship
steps: State the relationship: a Bird's home is a Nest
Same relationship: a Dog's home is a Kennel
boardDemo.teacherLine: Step 1: read pair 1 aloud. Step 2: say the relationship in one sentence. Step 3: apply that same sentence to pair 2. Never guess without saying the relationship first!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Pen : Write :: Scissors : ? — what does a pen do? Now apply the same to scissors.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Book : Read :: Fork : ? — state the relationship, then give the answer!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Exactly! A Book is used to Read, so a Fork is used to Eat. Perfect relationship spotting!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: ask yourself — what is a Book for? Reading. So what is a Fork for? Eating. The answer is Eat.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: Cow : Milk :: Hen : ? — state the relationship.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Some analogies are about categories: Rose is to Flower as Mango is to Fruit. Rose is a type of Flower — Mango is a type of Fruit. Member-to-category relationship!

boardDemo.title: Category Analogy — Part of a Group
steps: Relationship: Rose is a type of Flower (member : category)
Mango is a type of Fruit
boardDemo.teacherLine: The key question: is the first word a member (individual) and the second word the group (category)? Or the reverse? State that direction clearly before solving.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Cricket : Sport :: Piano : ? — Cricket is a type of Sport, so Piano is a type of…?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Sparrow : Bird :: Salmon : ? — what is the category that Salmon belongs to?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Sparrow is a type of Bird, so Salmon is a type of Fish. Category analogy cracked!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: ask — what group does a Sparrow belong to? Birds. Now ask — what group does a Salmon belong to? Fish!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: Chair : Furniture :: Shirt : ? — name the category.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Now numbers! 3 : 9 :: 4 : ? — what operation turns 3 into 9? Multiply by 3? Or square it? Find the operation, then apply it to 4!

boardDemo.title: Number Analogy — Find the Operation
steps: If question says 4:16, the operation is squaring.
boardDemo.teacherLine: When two operations both fit Pair 1, test both against Pair 2. Only one operation will match the answer choices. Always test the operation on Pair 1 first before applying to Pair 2.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: 5 : 25 :: 6 : ? — what operation was used on 5 to get 25? Test squaring.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: 7 : 49 :: 8 : ? — state the operation, then give the answer!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Spot on! 7 squared = 49, so 8 squared = 64. Number analogy solved in one step!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: 7 x 7 = 49 — that is squaring. Apply the same: 8 x 8 = 64.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: 10 : 100 :: 12 : ? — what operation and what answer?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Some number analogies use addition or subtraction patterns: 5 : 8 :: 11 : 14 — the rule is +3. Or they might use doubling: 4 : 8 :: 6 : 12. Find the rule!

boardDemo.title: Number Analogy — Additive and Multiplicative Patterns
boardDemo.teacherLine: Compute the difference (subtract) AND the ratio (divide) for Pair 1. Whichever gives a clean whole number is your rule. Apply to Pair 2.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: 9 : 18 :: 15 : ? — is the rule adding 9 or doubling? Test both on Pair 1.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: 7 : 21 :: 5 : ? — find the rule (is it multiply by 3?) then give the answer!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Brilliant! 7 x 3 = 21, so 5 x 3 = 15. Pattern analogy mastered!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: 21 divided by 7 = 3. The rule is multiply by 3. Apply: 5 x 3 = 15.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: 6 : 36 :: 7 : ? — is it multiply by 6 or squaring?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Letters can form analogies too! AC : EG :: IK : ? — notice each pair skips one letter (A-skip-C, E-skip-G). The gap in positions is +2. Apply the same to the second pair!

boardDemo.title: Letter Analogy — Forward Gap
steps: Pattern: two-letter pairs with internal gap +2
Next pair continues: M=13, O=15 — gap +2
boardDemo.teacherLine: Convert all letters to positions. Find the gap within the pair AND the gap between pairs. Both gaps must stay consistent. Then apply to find the missing pair.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: AB : CD :: EF : ? — what is the gap within the pair? What comes after EF in the same pattern?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: BD : FH :: JL : ? — convert to positions, check both gaps, give the answer!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! B=2,D=4 — F=6,H=8 — J=10,L=12 — next is N=14,P=16. Answer: NP. Letter analogy champion!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: within each pair, gap = +2. Between pair starts: B=2, F=6, J=10 — gap = +4 between starts. Next start: 10+4=14=N. Pair: N=14, P=16. Answer: NP.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: CE : GI :: KM : ? — give the answer.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Now the pairs run backwards! ZX : VT :: RP : ? — Z=26, X=24 (gap -2). V=22, T=20 (gap -2). The whole pattern moves backwards by 4 each time. Keep subtracting!

boardDemo.title: Letter Analogy — Backward Gap
steps: Pair 1: ZX — Z=26, X=24, internal gap = -2
Pair 2: VT — V=22, T=20, internal gap = -2 (same)
Gap between pair starts: Z=26, V=22, R=18 — gap = -4
boardDemo.teacherLine: Same method as forward — but gaps are negative. Convert to positions, subtract to find gaps. Apply the same subtraction to get the missing pair.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: YW : US :: QO : ? — check the internal gap and the between-pair gap, then give the answer.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: ZY : XW :: VU : ? — identify both gaps (they might be -1) and give the next pair!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Excellent! Z=26,Y=25 — X=24,W=23 — V=22,U=21 — next: T=20,S=19. Internal gap = -1. Answer: TS. Backward mastered!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: within each pair, consecutive letters with gap -1. Pair starts: Z=26, X=24, V=22 — gap = -2. Next start: 22-2=20=T. Pair: T=20, S=19. Answer: TS.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: ZX : VT :: RP : ? — give the answer.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Part-Whole analogies: Page : Book — a Page is a part of a Book. So Chapter : ? — a Chapter is also a part of a Book! Or try: Wheel : Car — a Wheel is a part of a Car.

boardDemo.title: Part-Whole — Member to Container
steps: Relationship: a Page is a part of a Book
A Chapter is also a part of a Book
boardDemo.teacherLine: Ask: is the first word a part of the second? Or a member of the second? Apply the exact same relationship direction to Pair 2.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Finger : Hand :: Toe : ? — a Finger is part of a Hand. So a Toe is part of…?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Petal : Flower :: Brick : ? — state the relationship, then give the answer!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! A Petal is a part of a Flower, so a Brick is a part of a Wall. Part-Whole analogy nailed!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: ask — what is made of petals? A Flower. Now ask — what is made of bricks? A Wall!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: Leaf : Tree :: Scale : ? — name the whole.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Tool-Purpose: a Pen is to Writing as a Knife is to Cutting. The tool is named first, the purpose (action) second. Find the purpose of the second tool!

boardDemo.title: Tool-Purpose — What Is It Used For?
steps: Relationship: a Pen is used for Writing
A Knife is used for Cutting
boardDemo.teacherLine: Ask: what is the first object used FOR? That is the purpose. Now name the purpose of the second object using the exact same sentence structure.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Camera : Photography :: Microscope : ? — a Camera is used for Photography. What is a Microscope used for?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Broom : Sweeping :: Needle : ? — what is a Needle used for?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Spot on! A Broom is used for Sweeping, so a Needle is used for Sewing. Tool-Purpose analogy solved!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: think of the main job of a Needle — it stitches cloth together. That action is Sewing.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: Ladder : Climbing :: Bridge : ? — what is a Bridge used for?

sessionFlow.coachHook: SPEED ROUND — all analogy types! For each pair, name the relationship type in 5 seconds, then give the answer in 10 seconds. Object, category, number, letter, part-whole, tool-purpose — you know them all. Go!

boardDemo.title: Speed Round — All Analogy Types
steps: Type 3 Letter: convert to positions, find both gaps
Type 4 Part-Whole: part is part of the whole
Type 5 Tool-Purpose: tool is used for the purpose
Speed tip: say the type name FIRST, then the answer
boardDemo.teacherLine: In competitive exams, the fastest solver wins. Identify the type in 3 seconds — you have practised all 5 types. Now speed is your weapon. Ready?

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Speed Q1: Lion : Pride :: Fish : ? Speed Q2: 3 : 27 :: 4 : ? Speed Q3: AC : CE :: EG : ? Go!
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Give all 3 answers and the relationship type for each!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: INCREDIBLE! Q1: Lion:Pride, Fish:Shoal (group/collective noun). Q2: 3 cubed=27, 4 cubed=64 (cube operation). Q3: letter pairs +2 gap, EG to GI (letter forward +2). ANALOGY CHAMPION!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick — Q1: a group of lions is a Pride, a group of fish is a Shoal. Q2: 27=3x3x3=3 cubed, so 4 cubed=64. Q3: A=1,C=3 to C=3,E=5 to E=5,G=7 — each pair starts 2 ahead: next is G=7,I=9 = GI.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Final: Rose : Red :: Grass : ? — and state the relationship type.
